title: Saturn at opposition
blurb: Saturn is closest and brightest for the year and visible all night in Pisces; its rings are nearly edge-on this season.

title: Mars meets Jupiter
blurb: Mars passes just over a degree from brilliant Jupiter in the pre-dawn eastern sky. Look 4 to 6 am local.

title: Mercury at its best (morning)
blurb: A favorable morning apparition: look for Mercury low in the east-southeast about 45 minutes before sunrise.

title: Supermoon (Beaver Moon)
blurb: The full Moon comes within a day of its closest point to Earth, rising around sunset looking slightly larger and brighter than usual.

title: Uranus at opposition
blurb: Uranus is at its best in Taurus; binoculars show a faint blue-green point near the Pleiades.

title: Closest supermoon of 2026 (Cold Moon)
blurb: The closest full Moon of the year, on the evening of December 23 local time.

title: Venus at its best as morning star
blurb: Venus stands farthest from the Sun, blazing high in the southeast before dawn.

title: Closest supermoon of 2027 (Wolf Moon)
blurb: The closest full Moon of 2027 rides very high in the winter sky all night.

title: Annular solar eclipse (South America)
blurb: The ring of fire crosses Chile and Argentina. Nothing is visible from North Dakota.

title: Jupiter at opposition
blurb: Jupiter is brightest for the year in Leo and up all night; for Medora this is the evening of February 10.

title: Mars at opposition
blurb: Mars reaches opposition in Leo, shining all night beside Jupiter, with closest approach to Earth the next day.

title: Penumbral lunar eclipse
blurb: A deep penumbral eclipse best seen from Europe and Africa. From Medora the Moon rises minutes before it ends, so the shading will be essentially undetectable.

title: Venus meets Saturn
blurb: Brilliant Venus passes just over half a degree from Saturn low in the eastern dawn sky. Look about an hour before sunrise on May 7 and 8.

title: Mercury at its best (evening)
blurb: A good spring evening apparition: Mercury sits low in the west-northwest 45 to 60 minutes after sunset.

title: Penumbral lunar eclipse (Pacific)
blurb: An extremely shallow eclipse visible from Asia, Australia and the Pacific. The Moon is below the horizon from Medora.

title: Total solar eclipse (Spain, North Africa)
blurb: The longest totality of the century on land crosses Spain, Egypt and Saudi Arabia. It happens before sunrise for North Dakota.

title: Penumbral lunar eclipse
blurb: The Moon slides through Earth's outer shadow from about 11:24 pm MDT on August 16 to 3:03 am, about 30 degrees up in the south. Expect a subtle grey shading on the Moon's northern edge near 1:14 am.

title: Saturn at opposition
blurb: Saturn is closest and brightest in Pisces and visible all night, with the rings beginning to open again.

title: Mercury at its best (morning)
blurb: A favorable morning apparition; Mercury is low in the east-southeast before sunrise.

title: Venus meets Mars
blurb: Venus, now an evening star, passes a third of a degree from faint Mars low in the southwest after sunset; the pair fits in one binocular field.

title: Uranus at opposition
blurb: Uranus is at its brightest in Taurus, a binocular object all night.

title: Partial lunar eclipse and supermoon
blurb: A small dark bite appears on the Moon's northern edge from 8:45 to 9:42 pm MST on the evening of January 11, with the Moon high in the east. It is also the first supermoon of 2028.

title: Annular solar eclipse (tiny partial at sunrise)
blurb: A ring-of-fire eclipse for South America and Spain. From Medora the Sun rises with a barely perceptible partial eclipse already ending. Never look at the Sun without proper eye protection.

title: Closest supermoon of 2028 (Snow Moon)
blurb: The closest full Moon of 2028, within hours of perigee.

title: Supermoon (Worm Moon)
blurb: The last supermoon of 2028 rises around sunset on the evening of March 10 local time.

title: Jupiter at opposition
blurb: Jupiter is brightest in Virgo and visible all night; a great time for its cloud belts and four big moons in binoculars.

title: Venus at its best as evening star
blurb: Venus is at its highest as the evening star, shining in the west for more than three hours after sunset.

title: Mercury at its best (evening)
blurb: A favorable spring evening apparition; look low in the west-northwest an hour after sunset.

title: Partial lunar eclipse (Eastern Hemisphere)
blurb: Visible from Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia; the Moon is below the horizon for all of North America.

title: Total solar eclipse (Australia, New Zealand)
blurb: Totality crosses Australia, including Sydney, and New Zealand. Not visible from the Americas.

title: Venus at its best as morning star
blurb: Venus is at its highest as a morning star, rising about three hours before the Sun.

title: Mercury at its best (morning)
blurb: A favorable morning apparition; Mercury is low in the east before dawn, with Jupiter nearby.

title: Mercury meets Jupiter
blurb: Mercury passes a degree from Jupiter low in the eastern dawn; a binocular challenge 40 minutes before sunrise.

title: Saturn at opposition
blurb: Saturn is closest and brightest and visible all night, with widening rings.

title: Venus meets Jupiter
blurb: The two brightest planets pass just over half a degree apart in the pre-dawn eastern sky, a spectacular naked-eye pairing on November 9 and 10.

title: Uranus at opposition
blurb: Uranus at its brightest in Taurus; binoculars or a small telescope all night.

title: Total lunar eclipse (Eastern Hemisphere)
blurb: A 72-minute totality for Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia. From Medora the Moon sets before the dark shadow arrives.
